To form the passato prossimo with AVERE: ho parlato, hai venduto, ha dormito.
To use the common irregular participles: fatto, visto, preso, letto, scritto, detto.

To tell the story of a weekend or a trip.
Monday, nine o'clock. Matei arrives at the workshop. Giulia is already there (for once!), with a coffee in her hand.
Good morning, Matei! So, what did you do at the weekend?
On Saturday I took the train and visited Siena.
How lovely! Did you see Piazza del Campo?
Yes, and I climbed the Torre del Mangia: four hundred steps!
Well done! And did you eat well?
Very well. I tasted pici and drank a fantastic red wine. And you?
I slept until noon and then cleaned the whole flat.
The whole flat? After the party?
Oh, yes. The neighbour's dog left a disaster. On Sunday I read a book on the sofa.
Good morning. Matei, have you already finished the report on Friday's painting?
Not yet, professor. I've started it, but I haven't finished it.
Then less Siena and more work. By noon, thank you.
(quietly) He said "thank you". That's a good sign!
Participles are stressed on the second-to-last syllable: man-JA-to, be-VOO-to, dor-MEE-to. Not: MAN-ja-to.
The double consonant is held a little longer, with a tiny pause before it: fat-to, let-to. "Leto" without the double would sound wrong.
The H is never pronounced: "ho" = "o", "hanno" = "an-no". It's only there to tell "ha" (has) apart from "a" (to).
SC + o / r = "sk", as in Romanian: SKOR-so, SKRIT-to. Only SC + e / i sounds "sh".

The passato prossimo is the main tense for completed actions in the past, like the Romanian perfect compus: "I ate / I have eaten" = "ho mangiato". It's formed with the present of AVERE + the verb's participle.
Just like Romanian: "am vorbit, ai vorbit, a vorbit". With AVERE the participle doesn't change: "Giulia ha parlato", "Le ragazze hanno parlato".
-ere verbs very often have an irregular participle (see section 3). "Bere" → "bevuto" (from the old form "bevere").
These have to be learned by heart. The good news: they are the same in all derived verbs (prendere → preso, so riprendere → ripreso too).
la settimana scorsa / il mese scorso / l'anno scorso
last week / last month / last year
due giorni fa / un anno fa
two days ago / a year ago
"Fa" comes AFTER the length of time: "tre giorni fa" = "three days ago". Not "fa tre giorni".
"Scorso" agrees: il mese scorso, la settimana scorsa, gli anni scorsi.
5. The negative, già and non… ancora
"Non" goes before AVERE: "Non ho mangiato." The adverbs "già" (already) and "ancora" (yet) usually go between AVERE and the participle:
The short answer: "Non ancora!" = "Not yet!". And "mai" = never: "Non ho mai visto Roma." = "I've never seen Rome."
6. The pronouns lo / la with the passato prossimo (for recognition)

In the dialogue Matei says "L'ho cominciata, ma non l'ho finita" (I've started it but haven't finished it). When a pronoun "lo / la" comes before AVERE, it becomes "l'" and the participle agrees with it. We'll work on this in detail in chapter 15; for now it's enough to recognise it.
I visited Rome three days ago.
Che cosa ha visitato Matei sabato?
Quanti scalini ha la torre del Mangia?
Che cosa ha fatto Giulia sabato?
Ha dormito e ha pulito la casa
Che cosa ha fatto Giulia domenica?
On Monday the teacher asked the children to write a diary of their Sunday. Pietro wrote three pages. Here they are.
"On Sunday morning I opened my eyes at seven. I looked outside: it was raining. So I woke Grandma up.
Grandma said: 'Today we're making ravioli.' We made the dough together. I broke the eggs and put the flour on the table. I also put flour on the floor, on the cat and in my hair.
Then Matei knocked at the door. He smelled the cooking and asked: 'Can I help?' Grandma answered: 'Yes, but wash your hands first.'
Matei had never made ravioli. He closed the first ten badly and the filling came out. Grandma laughed a lot. I took a photo for Matei's mum.
At lunch the three of us ate sixty ravioli. Michelangelo ate two ravioli that fell on the floor and then slept all afternoon on Matei's chair.
In the afternoon Matei taught me a Romanian word: 'delicios'. It means 'buonissimo'. I taught him to play scopa. I won, four times.
In the evening I had a bath to get the flour out of my hair. It was the best Sunday of the year."
The teacher read the diary and wrote in red: "Excellent! But who cleaned the floor?"
Che cosa hanno preparato Pietro e la nonna?
Dove ha messo la farina Pietro?
Sul tavolo, sul pavimento, sul gatto e sui capelli
Che parola romena ha imparato Pietro?
